context: linear · trench or duct bank → cable pulling → jointing → HV test; drum lengths and jointers govern

brief.intro: New to this project type? An underground cable circuit carries power between substations below the streets instead of on towers. The civil work — a trench or a concrete duct bank, with joint bays every few hundred metres — is most of the duration. The cable itself arrives on large drums, each made to a specific length for a specific section of the route, and is pulled in one drum at a time. Specialist jointers then make the joints and the terminations in clean, dry conditions; for high-voltage cable each joint takes days and only certified jointers may do it. The circuit is finished by a high-voltage test and by connection into the substations during an outage.

the pit where two drum lengths of cable are joined.
the length of cable on one drum; cut in the factory to suit the distance between joint bays.
the end fitting that connects the cable to switchgear, a transformer or an overhead line.
connecting the cable sheaths in a pattern, through link boxes, to cancel induced currents.

must_get_right: The route must be final before the cable is ordered: drum lengths are made for the distance between joint bays, and a change of route can make drums unusable.
Civil work is the long activity; cable can only be pulled into a section whose ducts are complete, cleaned and proved with a mandrel.
HV jointers are few. Count the joints and terminations, give each its real duration (days, not hours), and level the jointing teams — this is usually the resource-critical step.
The HV test set and the outage for connection are booked dates; missing them costs weeks.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by route section between joint bays, so each section shows civil complete, cable pulled, jointed and tested.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar; road works may be restricted to night or off-peak hours. Jointing continues without interruption once a joint is opened. Outage works are on the grid operator's dates.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Per section: permit → trench and ducts → mandrel proving → cable pulling → sheath test. Per joint bay: both adjoining sections pulled → jointing. Whole circuit: all joints and terminations → bonding checks → HV test → outage connection → energisation. The critical path runs through the cable delivery or the last civil section, then jointing and the HV test.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The route is frozen before the cable order; permits are granted section by section; the substations at both ends are ready for terminations; outage dates are granted as requested.

rows: HV XLPE cable (made to the drum schedule)
Before cable pulling in the first section

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy drums need access and a straight pulling set-up at each joint bay; pulling tension and bending radius limit section length; jointing needs dry, dust-free conditions.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: unknown services forcing a route change after drums are cut, late cable, duct damage found at mandrel stage, shortage of certified jointers, and a failed HV test. Contingency is held before the outage date.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by route section and joint bay; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the civil, pulling and jointing teams — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
